text_fidelity_a:
Garmin nüvi 265/265T 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Traffic I previously owned a Garmin Nuvi 360 which I loved. I specifically need a GPS that includes Bluetooth, since I use it both for directions and for hands-free phone use (which is rare, but important when I need it). I loved my 360 and used it daily until just a few months ago, when the Bluetooth suddenly stopped working. After troubleshooting with Garmin's tech support, it was determined the unit would need to be sent in for service, and since it was out of warranty, the flat charge for service was $79, which didn't include insured shipping costs.

Well, do the math. Obviously, one can acquire a brand-new GPS for not much more than $79, so I started shopping. That's how I ended up with my new Garmin Nuvi 265T. And I LOVE IT! I'm almost glad that my old unit went on the fritz, because it gave me an excuse to upgrade to this newer, fantastic unit.

The 360 was great for accurate directions, easy to see and read display, and consistent Bluetooth (until it broke). Here's how the 265T is even better:

- Smaller, lighter, and thinner, but with a slightly wider screen.
- No "antenna" on the back to flip up and fiddle with - it just works.
- Uses my existing mount (from ProClips), so no change to that was necessary.
- Includes FREE traffic notifications, which so far seem to work pretty well.
- When you power it on, it seems to bypass the warning screen that you need to "Agree" to quicker, and then shows a simple display: Where To, and View Map. On the 360, if you didn't do anything else, it would sit on the menu indefinitely, but the 265T automatically switches to map display after a few minutes if you don't select anything else. Basically, you can start your car and just forget about it, until you need it!

The traffic feature is ad-supported, so occasionally very small banner-type ads appear on the display, usually offering coupons for local restaurants etc. They are quite small and not intrusive in any way, so I don't mind them. I guess there's also an option to upgrade to a paid traffic service that would not include ads, but I don't see a need for that for my own use.

In general I am thrilled with Garmin products, and this Nuvi 265T is no exception. What a great deal, and a nice early Christmas present for myself!
text_fidelity_b: Garmin nüvi 265/265T 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Traffic

text_fidelity_a:
D-Link Wi-Fi Camera with Remote Viewing (DCS-930L) (Discontinued by Manufacturer) Compared to a similar camera made by Belkin, setting up the D-Link was kind of a pain. Not as much of a pain as setting up a Foscam F18918W - where you get directed to a third party domain name provider and get to learn the joys of port forwarding - but a relative hassle.

For the Belkin, I opened the box, plugged into my router, ran a set up program that took less than five minutes, downloaded an app, and I was up and running. While this is a very similar product in both look and function, it took over an hour - and two ethernet cables - to set it up. There is no Mac software on the installation cd. The box states that a Windows pc is required, but the website has a Mac download available. You have to scroll through the product photos, which aren't in alphanumeric order. Just keep looking until you find the DCS-930L - AFTER the 931L and the 932L and the 934L. Have faith. Keep going. It's there.

Once you get the program installed, it takes very little time to *find* the camera and teach it to log into your wireless network. And then you are back to the website to set up your account and view your camera. Except you are on a Mac, and the viewer requires you to install the Java Runtime Environment. JRE is a big old security vulnerability on Macs. So much so that Apple advises against using it. Mavericks lets you turn it on case by case - and, by default, it will ask you every time before running it. If you are on an OS below Mavericks, check the googles for setting your preferences so that you're not running JRE all the time.

Okay, so now you've got JRE going, and the first thing the program tells you is that you have to update your firmware AND you need to have the camera AND your computer ethernet-jacked right into your router. LOLWUT? I'm lucky. I am on a laptop, and I have an extra ethernet cable and an empty port. So, I did that, and there I was, up and running, about an hour, hour and a half, thereabouts, after I started.

Image quality is pretty good - not great. Audio is okay. The settings are very customizable. But the wifi receiver is very weak, and that limits the usefulness of this product.
text_fidelity_b: D-Link Wi-Fi Camera with Remote Viewing (DCS-930L) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

Sabrent Ultra Slim USB 3.0 To 2.5-Inch Sata Aluminum Screwless Hard Drive Enclosure Blue (EC-RDBL) I love how compact this case is. The rounded edges make the case seem even smaller.
I'm not going to section off the Good, Bad, Ugly features because I really haven't found any real problems with this enclosure.

Features I like:
- Fits 2.5" notebook HDD at the standard height (not necessary to buy a low profile SSD)
- Plug and Play. Some enclosures take almost a minute for the PC to recognize. The drive shows up instantly in My Computer once plugged in.
- Fast USB 3.0. I'll go into this in more detail.
- Aluminum case. Good for keeping the drive cool.
- Opens without a tool. A button (a little hard to press) releases the top and bottom covers allowing easy access to the drive inside.
- Led is not too bright. The LED is hidden behind black translucent plastic so it doesn't get too bright. Just enough for you to see that it is on and the drive is reading.

Speed:
I boot Windows 8.1 To Go from a standard 5400rpm drive plugged in to this enclosure. Windows To Go contains the entire windows OS and boots it from USB which allows a computer to dual boot to Windows 8.1 by simply plugging the drive in. From this drive, I've also installed and played games like Assassin's Creed Unity and Shadows of Mordor. While loading speed may be slower than an SSD plugged in to SATA, I still felt that the loading speed for the games were acceptable.

In conclusion, this is a nice looking case that feels good to hold, easy to slip in to a pocket and easily accessible (I switch out the drives sometimes). It is fully supported by Windows 8 and is sold at a great price.

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung SSD 860 EVO 4TB 2.5 Inch SATA III Internal SSD (MZ-76E4T0B/AM) I have built systems with SSDs for the last several years and I have come to see where they have their strengths and weaknesses. Not all SSDs are the same, and some have distinct advantages over others though the gap is definitely narrowing. This is my first experience with Samsung’s SSDs, and so far it has been a very positive experience. It has given me no issues at all and has performed well.

I installed the drive in a Dell Inspiron laptop which was running Windows 8. On the SSD, I installed Linux instead. Installation was very smooth, it was quick and I had a working system up and running in no time. I have now been running the system constantly for over a week (no powering off or hibernating) and the drive has shown no signs of trouble.

I loaded up a virtual machine and ran it on top of the main installation. The VM and the host install both have performed admirably and have not suffered from any noticeable I/O lag. Running smartctl against the drive after the past week of testing, it has reported no errors and a very healthy drive across the board.

Aside from the speed advantages of an SSD over a platter-based drive, this drive is absolutely silent (no surprise there) and so far I have not had any heat issues. It has given me no indications of any trouble in operation and my system is running as smoothly as should be expected.

The one issue I have with this drive, and it’s not a performance or quality issue, is the pricing. It is a little more expensive than most, and so far I have not seen any real justification for it over the likes of Crucial, Kingston or other branded drives. There may be justifiable reasons that reveal themselves later (I do not know how long this drive will continue to work but it should literally last for several years, even under very heavy use), but for now it seems a tad expensive compared to competitors.

Operationally I cannot find fault with this drive. It works well, it’s fast and quiet (as should be expected) and so far I’ve not had heat issues with it. Utilities I have run against it have shown that the drive is very healthy and has reported no problems out of the box. This is a good drive that will serve well. Time will tell, though, if it is worth the slightly higher asking price.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung SSD 860 EVO 4TB 2.5 Inch SATA III Internal SSD (MZ-76E4T0B/AM)

text_fidelity_a:
Asus Nexus 7 2B32 7-Inch 32 GB Tablet, Black (2013 Model) 7 May 2014: Thanks to Google's omission of full USB OTG function, file transfers are frustrating & sometimes impossible. When I return home, I'm rooting it.

After 24 hours, I like it. It's a little different from my Galaxy Player 5 inch. The extra processor speed is nice. So is the combination of the light weight and larger screen. The GP5 was getting bogged down by software bloat. It fits nicely in my old K3 case. So far, so good.

...and it works with my Targus Bluetooth keyboard. Actually, it works better than it does with the GP5. The Samsung has some key-mapping problems, probably due to Gingerbread.

As to reading, I happened to be starting a novel the other day, and started it on the Nexus 7. I had no problem. I did keep the brightness on 'Auto', so the light level of the screen matched the ambient light. With the GP5, matching light levels was a little chancy, so I had a bit more eyestrain. (Of course the extra 2" of screen have no bearing on that, right?)

I did try the freebie 'La Luna' video that Google gives away. It watched fine on the 7" screen. The thing I really like is that there is a 7" screen in the weight of a past-technology 5" package. I owned a Nook color for 13 days, but took it back because of the weight and balance. It just wasn't comfortable to hold.

I haven't tried any significant music listening. I suspect I'll still prefer my Clip+ for that. The Nexus is a little large for that purpose. I also haven't tried the camera in any particular serious way. A selfie and a picture of my cat isn't much of a trial. Again, I'll probably use a purpose-made camera for real pictures. I also haven't explored portability yet. In the case, it's a bit bulky for easy transport, whereas the GP5 fits in my pocket next to my cell phone. I probably won't put the N7 in my pocket without a case. It's a little large and fragile seeming for that.

...As to the camera, it's OK, the image quality is fine, but a 7" tablet just isn't a good ergonomic platform for picture taking. This is the best from an afternoon at Mass Audubon's Ipswich River Wildlife Sanctuary.

Picture is available at:
MobileRead Forums > E-Book Readers > Android Devices>Nexus 7 2013 1st Impressions

...And I still prefer my Clip+ for music. I hand to hunt around the Android store for a decent player for my collection which includes WMAs as well as MP3s. Google does not play WMAs (cue prissy, superior sniff). I settled on Poweramp, not because it was perfect, but because it was the first one I came to that was good enough. I just want to listen to some music, people, not commit my soul to a single, ringing, crystalline-pure music player that rules them all. Sheesh.

Someday I may do a better review, too. All of the usual things about tablets are at worst adequate on the N7.

Oh, one piece of free advice, worth every penny you paid: Don't go hog wild buying really great accessories. Shop around. A $3 wire easel from a craft store will make a fine desk stand. I have one at work and one at home. A chopstick and a binder clip will do in a pinch. Also, there are good $10 EVA zip cases that will protect your N7 for transport. They don't have to be purpose built. My old K3 had a case that loosely fits the N7 (freebie!) and my KPW1 lives in a similar case. As to ear buds, the candy-colored $5 ones in the bin at the cash register at WalGreens are my favorite, and you never misplace them, because candy-colored.
text_fidelity_b: Asus Nexus 7 2B32 7-Inch 32 GB Tablet, Black (2013 Model)

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Zen Sleek Photo 20 GB Multimedia Player (Aluminum/White) I was in the market for a hard drive-based music player and didn't want to go the normal iPxx route, so I began checking into different brands. I had a list of criteria that the player had to meet:

-EXCELLENT SOUND. This is critical. A SnR (Signal to Noise Ratio) of 95db or better

-Excellent battery life. At least 15 hours

-At least 20 GB

-A color screen

-Sturdy build

-As little touch-sensitive controlling as possible. Click wheels are inaccurate and bothersome.

-Ease of use. Drag and drop is preferred.

-AC adapter for charging on the road or from an AC converter in a car

This player meets all of those needs. The SnR is 97db, I've gotten 18 hours out of the battery (remember that increased settings like equalizers and higher bitrates mean lower battery life for ALL players), the case is solid and brushed aluminum, the screen is pretty and quite sharp, only one touch-sensitive control is present, the player CAN drag and drop through Win XP, and it comes with a wall adapter.

I love the powerful sound this puts out and it can drive my big headphones with no problem. It can, like most HDD players, set aside a partition for storage. It has a good FM tuner, recording of FM and a little mic for voice notes. It can even sync with Outlook for contacts and other info. The hard disk seems fast and

Now for the drawbacks:

-You can't watch 15fps video on a tiny screen and reduce your battery life by 67%

-The USB cable is proprietary...no mini USB!

-The wall charger cable plugs into the USB cable...this means two cables for recharging from the wall

-Looking at photos and playing music at the same time is not possible

-Creative software is always iffy. Thankfully, in Win XP, you can open the player from My Computer and access its contents directly with non-DRM music and photos.

-Battery is NON-USER REPLACEABLE. This is odd for Creative.

-No mention of this on the Creative website. Thankfully, updated drivers ARE available from support.

This player would have been state-of-the-art about a year ago, but has been eclipsed by its bigger brother the Zen Vision with 30 and 60GB drives and video...however, if you're not buying into the "kill your eyes with tiny video on tiny screens" and just want a SOLID and RELIABLE player with booming sound, this is it!!! You can tell it's custom-made for Windows (it's MTP, not UMS for any computer), but if you're running XP, then it's a solid choice because you can skip the Creative software and just load music on it.

If you can get it on sale like I did, snatch it up. This is a little gem of a player!
text_fidelity_b: Creative Zen Sleek Photo 20 GB Multimedia Player (Aluminum/White)

text_fidelity_a:
3MP Wireless Security Camera System, Dragon Touch 8CH NVR 4pcs WiFi Security Cameras Outdoor with Color Night Vision, AI Human Detection, Motion Alert, Remote Access, IP66 Waterproof Cameras, No HDD Prior to getting this NVR system, I had already started researching on POE switches. For some reason, I assumed all NVR cameras are POE. I knew this Dragon Touch NVR had no POE ports in the back, but it didn't matter because I had planned to use POE switches. If you're a newbie like me, here are some noteworthy things before you make your decision:

1. The four cameras in this set comes with four power adapters. I thought how nice of them to include this option. But as it turns out, this is NOT an option. You need to use the power adapters for each camera. I learned that getting POE switches is only half the battle, the other half is making sure the cameras are POE compatible. I didn't know that. I thought POE switches would allow me to get rid of power adapters to any camera, any brand. Sadly, this is not the case. So this Dragon Touch system is designed for wi-fi. You only need to hook up the power adapter to each camera. But the whole point of me going to NVR is to use ethernet for more dependable connections. You can still do that with this system, but you'll still need to connect the power adapters, so you're running two cables for each camera. Had I known that, I would not have gotten this system.

2. You can use other brand cameras with this NVR if the cameras are ONVIF. However, I'm betting they still need to be the non-POE kind. I'm trying to connect a H.View POE camera, but I'm getting a black screen. Dragon Touch said that model is not compatible. End of email. I had to follow up with "What POE cameras are compatible?" I'll update when they respond.

3. It goes without saying, but in case you don't know, you need to connect NVR to a monitor for viewing. The back of the NVR has options for VGA or HDMI out. Alternatively, you can view via their Homeviz app.

4. No hard drive is included, but a hard drive is not necessary for you to start learning, testing, and setting things up. You can live view without a hard drive, but to record you'll need to install a hard drive.

5. Lastly, I'll talk about the build quality of this system. The Dragon Touch is very professionally packaged, the NVR is small and light, but that's without a hard drive currently. The cameras feel real nice, has good heft to them. I am not going to subtract any stars because of my newbie assumptions. As a matter of fact, I'm learning that if you want NVR systems with POE cameras, they would be much more expensive than what you're paying here. If I can figure a way to run both ethernet and power adapters, I may end up using this system. However, I will subtract a star for the lack of info in their listing, and emails. A product like this should clearly state whether or not their cameras are POE, and whether or not the NVR can handle POE cameras. 4-Stars.
text_fidelity_b: 3MP Wireless Security Camera System, Dragon Touch 8CH NVR 4pcs WiFi Security Cameras Outdoor with Color Night Vision, AI Human Detection, Motion Alert, Remote Access, IP66 Waterproof Cameras, No HDD

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech HD Webcam C525, Portable HD 720p Video Calling with Autofocus - Black [[VIDEOID:132a9e1a9608d7ddcfd6e870320f72aa]] The 75 second video is intended as a supplement to the written review so that you can see for yourself how well my fairly standard computer can record 720p, and thus get an idea if your computer can benefit from a 720p recording device. This is important to consider because even the manufacturer mentions that many computers cannot keep up with the recording. I mention my system specs in the video.

It's a well designed webcam. It is very small, and the ability to protect its own lens is great. They supply ~5 ft. cord that - wrapped up - takes up about as much room as the camera itself, which allows a connection between a desktop and a separate monitor. Better would have been if they used a standard micro USB connector or some kind of cord wrap system to keep all that out of your way and allow you to use a 30cm cord for connection to your laptop.

The actual optics seem great and the autofocus works pretty well. Even Win XP SP2 allowed me to use the camera function (no video) immediately without installing any software. The software that comes with it eats up nearly 300MB of ROM (that includes their own calling application and editing software that you don't need to install) and only tries caducously to take over your computer (a registry edit and startup menu delete gets rid of unwanted reminders and useless junk running in the background). Oh...I noticed one typo in their software, which is unacceptable, and it also keeps telling me that it doesn't recognize the mic (which is built into the camera), but it records sound anyway.

The design allows for mounting on a monitor 26mm thick or less, but I suppose you could sort of lay it on top of a CRT monitor with no problems. It also allows for a fairly stable mounting on a laptop.

Great device that I would recommend, but I had to take off a star for less than perfect portability and some software blips.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech HD Webcam C525, Portable HD 720p Video Calling with Autofocus - Black

Case Logic KDH-101 Kontrast DSLR Zoom Holster (Black) Here's the bottom line: I compared this case with the Amazon Basics case, and frankly found the latter to be comparable or even slightly better (at a much lower price).

This is a pretty nice case for a DSLR wearing a zoom lens. I have a Nikon D5300 which I usually pack with a 18-200mm zoom lens on it, and have found the Amazon case to be satisfactory for holding the camera+zoom and the lens hood in the main compartment, and the battery charger and of course a spare chip in the side pckets. There's room in a side pocket to carry a small card reader if I want to bring that as well.

The Case Logic case is very similar, and if I had gotten it first I would probably have been quite satisfied. However, I found that the suspension "hammock" for the camera didn't work quite as well in practice as it does in theory. The camera isn't symmetric of course, and more of it seems to slip through the hole than is intended, and it lies in it at an angle. I also found that I couldn't quite as easily put the lens hood on top as I have gotten used to doing with the Amazon case.

Otherwise, this is well made, with sturdy looking and smoothly functioning zippers, robust strap & handle, and functional side pockets. Certainly a good product, you won't regret buying this case, other than possible regret over the price paid. (Note that I haven't owned the cases long enough to comment on any durability differences.)
text_fidelity_b: Case Logic KDH-101 Kontrast DSLR Zoom Holster (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Brainwavz S1 IEM Noise Isolating Earphones With Clearwavz Remote and Microphone for iPhone iPad iPod I’m really impressed with these earphones. Usually with mid-priced earphones you have to qualify the sound with the phrase “for the price.” Not with these – they put out sound that rivals earbuds I have that cost 3 to 4 times more.

The clarity is spot-on. Nice crisp treble and midrange, but not at the expense of a goodly amount of bass. Not skull-shaking bass, but clean, non-boomy bass that rounds out the sound perfectly.

The overall build quality is excellent. It does have a potentially polarizing feature: a flat cable. Personally, I really like the flat cable. The style is helpful in keeping the earbuds in place (since these are over-the-ear style buds) and helps keep cord tangles to a minimum. There’s also a small slider on the cable yoke that can be adjusted to keep them secure when wearing them while in motion. However, others who have borrowed these from me were not as enthused about the flat cable. No one hated it, but the reaction was occasionally on the lukewarm side.

Wearing comfort is another point where these excel. Lightweight, nice ear canal feel, and solid sound isolation. It comes with a variety of tips to ensure a good fit for pretty much anyone. I’d suggest trying a variety of sizes since bass response and sound isolation are affected by how well these fit in your ears.

Also included is a nicely styled case that holds the earbuds plus the accessory tips. It’s well-made, attractive and designed for actual use, with small mesh pockets to hold things in place.

The 3.5mm plug is angled to make it easy to use plus stay out of the way better than the conventional straight type plug when using it on a small mp3 player.

Try as I might, I can’t come up with a single negative about these. Built well, sounds great, and thoughtful design touches throughout. Collectively, that makes these one of the best values in earbuds I’ve run across so far, and I would highly recommend them.

That happened to me several times on my job with my other backpacks and it was really frustrating. It's very easy to set your backpack down on the ground not realizing the area is wet.

The shoulder straps are padded and adjustable, and it has a waist strap for extra stability. Even if you didn't use this backpack to tote your 17" marvel of technology around, it would serve well as a camper/hiker backpack. I can't wait to start using it. If something should go wrong or tear up, I will most definitely update this review telling about it, but for now I can find no fault whatsoever with it.

text_fidelity_a:
Display Port to HDMI Converter with Audio Adapter I wanted to hear and see Skype on our Sony XBR7 HDMI-only capable 1080p TV, fed from a Lenovo X220 convertable laptop/tablet running System 7 64 bit Ultimate through the DisplayPort. I also wanted to watch some YouTube videos playing from Firefox and hear their audio on my big living room audio system. No such luck.

When first plugged in, I remember briefly seeing the TV via this DisplayPort adapter in the audio device list, but the next time, the TV disappeared and is nowhere to be found. Not in the audio control panel, anyway. It's just gone.

I first chalked this up to the Thinkpad weirdness, as its internal audio card/mic doesn't work with Skype either. If I plug in an external Logitech webcam, it works seamlessly. Internal camera/mic, nothing.

Sony audio problems aside, the video looks great on the big screen, though it overscans a bit and cuts off part of the menu bar at the bottom.

One reviewer said he could see his TV in the list of audio devices and was able to configure its audio to satisfaction. My Sony TV does not show in the Lenovo audio devices list, though it does show as a generic PnP monitor.

I plugged the HDMI cable into a tiny 7" video monitor and whatdayaknow, the audio came through and the device showed up as an audio device. Then I plugged it into a 20" Vizio and sure enough, it works fine too. Same with a Samsung LCD. Three monitors out of four work. The Sony is the only one that doesn't. Hmmmm.

Sooooo, I'm guessing there's something about Sony's DRM or some other HDMI protocol blocking the computer from seeing the TV. I set all the TVs for internal speakers. Routing audio to an external amp is another variable in the equation.

Nothing wrong with the adapter that I can tell, it simply doesn't see certain Sony TV's.
text_fidelity_b: Display Port to HDMI Converter with Audio Adapter
